_meta.title: AI Challenge of the Week
_meta.rotationNote: Weekly rotation by ISO calendar week. After week 12 it restarts at week 1. The next twelve challenges are prepared by week 10.

challenges.role: HR lead at an 80-person engineering company
challenges.scenario: Three days for a salary benchmark against five competitors, says the CFO. Public sources only, such as company reports, job listings and employee-submitted salary data. Two hours for the first analysis, no data analyst. How do you get to a defensible draft?
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Write the brief with the analyst role, the company and region, and five output columns for competitor, role and level, reported salary range, source and confidence. 2. Collect a small, documented set of public records per competitor. Respect site terms and never present estimates as payroll facts. 3. Have Claude extract the ranges and mark missing or uncertain values. 4. Pick the three claims that most need a manual check. 5. Verify them at the original sources, record the sample limits and export the reviewed table for the CFO.
rubric: The brief states the role, context and output format
Named public sources replace an undefined web search
Sample sizes and source limitations are recorded
Uncertain values carry an explicit confidence label
A critical review happens before delivery
The output format matches the table the CFO needs
The two-hour limit applies to a bounded first analysis, not a complete compensation study

challenges.role: Sales lead at a 45-person trade business
challenges.scenario: 230 open quotations in the system, some 90 days old. Nobody knows which are still live. Checking them all by hand takes an estimated three days. How do you build a review queue in two hours?
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Export only what triage needs, which is customer reference, value, last activity and status. Personal data runs through the organisation's approved process. 2. Define review classes such as HOT, WARM, COLD and DEAD with explicit age and value thresholds. 3. Have follow-up drafts written for a person to approve; nothing goes out automatically. 4. The highest-priority records get a personal call, the rest go into review queues. Never archive on a model recommendation alone. 5. Compare the rules with actual outcomes every week.
rubric: Data is exported from the source system instead of retyped
Triage classes use explicit, reviewable thresholds
Each class has an appropriate draft template in plain business language
A person reviews every high-value follow-up
The two-hour limit covers triage setup and drafts
A recurring review replaces a one-off cleanup
Customer data is processed only through an approved data-protection and access-control path

challenges.scenario: Eight metrics, four departments, twelve commentary lines. The monthly report has taken six hours so far. Today a colleague is out and you have 90 minutes. How do you get to a reviewable draft?
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Set up a controlled workspace and add the last three reports as structure and style references. 2. Put the current raw figures in front of it as a validated table. 3. Ask for the same structure, stated variance calculations and commentary that separates fact from hypothesis. 4. Recalculate every reported figure in Excel and check the cited source cell. 5. Investigate two or three material variances and record several possible explanations instead of one unevidenced cause. 6. Export the reviewed document in the required format.
rubric: Previous reports provide a structure and style reference
Every figure is checked independently of generated prose
Variance rules are fixed before the draft
Possible explanations are labelled as hypotheses
Verification gets more time than wording
The final format matches management's reporting process
The workspace and checks can be reused next month

challenges.role: Executive assistant at a 200-person software company
challenges.scenario: Tomorrow morning an executive flies to an investor meeting. By tonight you need an eight-page briefing on three competitors, covering public financial information, product positioning, management, recent announcements and an evidence-based risk assessment.
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Fix the eight pages before any research, so one page of summary, two per competitor and one comparison page. 2. Collect the same source categories for every competitor in parallel, with publication dates and direct links. 3. Have Claude draft against the template and mark every uncertain statement. 4. Check financial figures and quotations in the original documents. 5. Compare the competitors on financial strength, delivery pace, team and product, and back every rating. 6. Export the reviewed briefing and a one-page meeting reference.
rubric: The structure stands before drafting starts
Every competitor is researched against the same source plan
The writing follows an approved internal example rather than generic consulting language
Financial figures and quotations are checked at the source
The comparison matrix separates evidence from judgement
The deliverables are the briefing and a concise meeting reference
The four-hour plan limits scope while reserving time for verification

challenges.role: IT lead at a 60-person family business
challenges.scenario: Management asks where AI would be worth it. Next week you present a first concept. Budget open, time short, no established AI practice in the company. Where do you start?
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Day 1: build a broad, industry-specific list of candidate use cases and strike every candidate without a clear process owner or data path. 2. Day 2: ask eight people from different functions five short questions about recurring work and failure points. Have Claude cluster the answers, then check each cluster against the original responses. 3. Day 3: compare the remaining cases on effort, number of staff affected, data sensitivity, operational risk and time to evidence. 4. Put two candidates forward with assumptions, exclusions, required controls and the next validation step. Any return estimate is a range built from named inputs, never a promised result.
rubric: External use-case research is combined with employee evidence
Claude supports clustering and structure, not the final decision
Effort, reach, risk and evidence time are explicit criteria
Management gets two prioritised candidates, not a long list
The output fits on one decision page
Each candidate has a concrete validation step and owner
The work runs across three days so sources can be checked

challenges.role: Marketing lead at a 30-person B2B software company
challenges.scenario: Three posts a week for 13 weeks: the Q3 LinkedIn calendar on AI-native teams. There is no agency budget, and nobody but you is on it.
challenges.timeBudget: 1 day for the Q3 plan plus 30 minutes per week for drafting
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Analyse the last 30 posts and the performance data you have, then derive three repeatable formats. Small samples do not establish causation. 2. Generate topic candidates for a German B2B audience and pick 39 relevant ones without duplicates. 3. For every topic, fix the factual angle and the evidence it needs before any hook or call to action. 4. The quarterly calendar names owner, source status and review date. 5. Write three drafts a week, edited for factual accuracy and company voice. 6. Review performance monthly and record what you changed.
rubric: Earlier posts shape the style without being copied
Performance data informs selection with its limitations recorded
The calendar contains exactly 39 topics for 3 posts across 13 weeks
An angle and evidence requirement precede each draft
The weekly 30 minutes cover drafting; review time is planned separately
A monthly review creates a documented feedback loop
The language is precise and appropriate for a German B2B audience

challenges.scenario: Three competing feature requests from customers. The next sprint has room for one. How do you decide, and how do you document it?
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Record every request with the customer's context and the relevant product-usage data. 2. For each feature, note the user problem, affected segments and any existing substitute. 3. Build a RICE table with written definitions for reach, impact, confidence and effort. Claude does the arithmetic only after the inputs are checked. 4. For every estimate on thin evidence, name one small research step that would improve it. 5. Record decision, assumptions and rejected alternatives. 6. After release, compare actual use and outcomes with the estimates.
rubric: A defined method replaces an undocumented preference
Product-usage evidence is included
Confidence is explicit and tied to evidence
Thin-evidence assumptions get a research action
The decision and rejected alternatives are recorded
A post-release measurement point is defined
Claude structures and calculates; the accountable owner decides

challenges.role: Compliance officer at a medium-sized financial company
challenges.scenario: Management wants an AI chat assistant in customer advice. Two weeks to say whether the plan can proceed, and under which conditions. GDPR, the EU AI Act and sector rules can all apply at once.
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Describe the proposed system, the user journey, decision effects, data categories, model provider and the human role. 2. Check each legal framework separately against primary sources, so GDPR legal basis, minimisation and DPIA; role and risk classification under the EU AI Act; applicable financial-supervision requirements. 3. Build a traceable list of requirements, evidence and open questions. 4. Qualified legal and compliance owners review the analysis. 5. Produce a decision matrix with permitted scope, prohibited uses, required contracts, controls, tests and training. 6. Record the recommendation and its conditions. Model output is not legal advice.
rubric: The analysis covers GDPR, the EU AI Act and applicable sector rules separately
Primary sources support the summary
A qualified legal or compliance review is mandatory
The decision matrix distinguishes permitted scope, exclusions and conditions
Required evidence such as contracts, assessments and training records is named
Management gets a conditional recommendation, not a binary model answer
Risk classification and assessment decisions are documented for later audit

challenges.role: HR lead at a 500-person industrial company
challenges.scenario: 370 applications in ten days for five vacancies. The team manages 20 a day and needs a lawful triage process by Friday. How do you cut the administrative work without handing employment decisions to a model?
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Before a model is involved, the hiring owners define measurable requirements, evidence rules and prohibited proxy criteria for each role. 2. Confirm the legal basis, retention, access controls, provider contract, applicable EU AI Act classification and any required impact assessment. 3. Use AI only for approved administrative support, such as pulling evidence into a review table. Applications are never ranked or rejected automatically. 4. Recruiters read the source application and decide every case. 5. Test for extraction errors and disparate outcomes, edge cases included. 6. Keep an audit trail and give applicants the required information and rights process.
rubric: Job-related criteria and prohibited proxies are defined before processing
Legal basis, EU AI Act classification and impact-assessment duties are checked
The model never ranks or rejects on its own
A recruiter checks source evidence and decides every case
Accuracy and bias tests include documented edge cases
Retention, access and applicant-rights processes are recorded
The output is a review table with source references, not an unexplained score

challenges.role: Sales engineer at an enterprise B2B software company
challenges.scenario: Ten days for a technical proof of concept with your system and access to the customer's database. Work like this normally takes six weeks. Do you accept, and with what scope and controls?
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Day 1: search the internal repository for comparable proof-of-concept work and record the reusable components with licence, owner and test state. 2. Days 1 and 2: agree five observable user stories, a data-access boundary, acceptance criteria and explicit exclusions. 3. Days 3 to 7: build and test in an isolated environment, and review the generated code and its dependencies. 4. Day 8: internal security and operations review of authentication, audit logs, rate limits, secrets and teardown. 5. Day 9: rehearse the demonstration and the failure path. 6. Day 10: show the agreed scope and record what production would still need.
rubric: Existing components are checked for reuse, not assumed away
Scope is limited to five observable user stories
A person reviews the generated code and tests
Authentication, audit logging, rate limits, secrets and teardown are checked
An internal dry run occurs before the customer session
The proof of concept is explicitly separated from a production commitment
The ten-day schedule has owners, review gates and exclusions

challenges.role: Office manager at a 40-person law firm
challenges.scenario: 120 client emails a day. 40 percent concern existing matters, 30 percent ask for appointments, 20 percent are new enquiries, 10 percent are spam or sales. Two people cannot keep pace. How do you cut the handling work without exposing privileged information or sending unreviewed legal communications?
challenges.timeBudget: 1 week for setup plus continuous improvement
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Before choosing a model, settle what confidentiality, professional secrecy, retention and access require. Local execution can reduce transfers; alone it proves no compliance. 2. Build an isolated n8n workflow that sorts example or approved messages into four queues. 3. Appointment and acknowledgement messages stay drafts until authorised staff release them. 4. Route existing-matter and ambiguous messages to the responsible team without adding generated legal advice. 5. Keep spam handling reversible during evaluation. 6. Review classification errors weekly and update the tests before the prompts. 7. Document the assessment, provider and processor roles, staff procedure and client information duties with qualified counsel.
rubric: The architecture follows confidentiality and professional-secrecy requirements
Classification supports routing and does not make legal decisions
Authorised staff release every template before sending
Ambiguous messages and existing matters have a fixed path
A weekly error review updates a fixed test set
The legal assessment and data-protection controls are documented
Client transparency duties are assessed with qualified counsel

challenges.scenario: Planning for 2027 fills 200 spreadsheet rows across targets, budget and team growth. It used to take two weeks. You want two days without lowering the review standard. How do you cut the work down?
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Day 1, morning: compare the last three plans with actual results and find the categories with repeated forecast error. 2. Day 1, afternoon: record the 2027 assumptions with source, owner and confidence, then build a base, a downside and an upside scenario. 3. Day 2, morning: functional leads challenge the assumptions and open risks get written down. Claude can structure the discussion; it cannot validate a business assumption. 4. Day 2, afternoon: finish the controlled workbook and a one-page summary per scenario. 5. Schedule quarterly plan-to-actual checks. Two days is a bounded process target, not a guarantee of equal quality.
rubric: Earlier plan-to-actual gaps feed calibration
Base, downside and upside scenarios use stated assumptions
Functional leads challenge the assumptions
Each scenario has a one-page decision summary
Quarterly reviews compare actual results with the plan
Claude structures analysis; the managing director remains accountable
The two-day target preserves explicit verification and sign-off gates
